blocks.heading: Benefits and limits of specialisation
blocks.text: Specialisation can improve skill through repetition, reduce time spent changing tasks and allow equipment to be used intensively. These gains may raise output or reduce unit costs if the stages are coordinated and demand supports the output. Limitations include repetitive work, dependence on other stages and a loss of flexibility. A specialised skill or product may become less useful when demand changes. Skills for cover can be developed through on-the-job or off-the-job training; the choice of training method is explained in Topic 3.5, while the point here is continuity between specialised tasks.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Added a scope-limited cross-reference naming on-the-job and off-the-job training. Re-read the unchanged integrated bakery answers: their division-of-labour, trade and cover reasoning remains valid; no training-method preference was added.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Omuti Foods has steady orders for standard loaves but is considering accepting many individually decorated celebration breads. A task-based line suits repeated standard loaves because workers can practise a narrow activity and organise batches efficiently. It may be less suitable when orders differ substantially or one absent worker stops a stage. A sensible judgement is to specialise the repeated standard work while retaining flexible skills for varied orders. If most demand becomes individual orders, that balance should change.
